Area.evidence_source: Amid reports that Western males suicide at 3 times the rate of females, socially constructed and normative masculinities have offered important insights toward better understanding this long-standing pattern. Within this literature, social isolation and linkages to masculine ideals have been highlighted as complicit in this complex social problem. There have been consistent arguments regarding men's alignments to normative masculine constructions—including stoicism and emotional restraint—and their role in the production of social isolation and, eventually, pathways to suicide. Oliffe, Galdas, Han, and Kelly (2013), for example, described how Canadian college men's alignments to solitary discourses could pass as normative male behavior rather than self-isolating practices flowing from, and contributing to, the participant's depression, psychological distress, and suicidality. A study of Australian men by Player et al. (2015) highlighted how men's stoicism and self-reliance was enmeshed in participants' experiences of social isolation (in this case, articulated as isolation from significant others), contributing to mood disorders, inadequate decision making, and, eventually, suicidality. In this work, isolation produced a cascade of negative events and starkly contrasted the protections afforded against suicidality to men who were connected to family, friends, and social networks (Player et al., 2015). Ramirez and Badger's (2014) U.S. study reported "disconnecting" processes among men experiencing suicidality wherein participants withdrew from themselves, family, and friends through high-risk behaviors and aggression to numb their emotional pain (p. 24).
